students.title: Students
students.goal: Get a new singer to sing one note in Pitch Perfect, turn that into a small habit, then show the deeper layer (coaching feedback, courses, mentorship) only after they have felt value.
students.trigger: Student account created in the app.
students.audience: Self-taught singers and artists who do not know if they are actually improving.
students.cta_note: Gold buttons. Every CTA lands inside the app.

leads.title: Student Leads
leads.goal: Deliver the pitch guide the website already promises, teach one thing, then convert the reader into a free account. Three emails, then stop.
leads.trigger: Email submitted through the exit-intent popup or the footer form without creating an account.
leads.audience: Visitors who were curious but not ready to sign up.
leads.cta_note: Gold buttons. Every CTA goes to student signup. If they create an account, move them to the Students track and stop this one.

teachers.title: Teachers & Studios
teachers.goal: Turn a demo request into a booked walkthrough, then into a three-student pilot, and close the loop cleanly when a coach goes quiet. Concierge tone, sold through the coach's own workflow pain.
teachers.trigger: Teacher demo form submitted on the website (or a teacher email captured without a demo request).
teachers.audience: Independent vocal coaches and studio owners whose students say they practiced, but who cannot see what actually happened.
teachers.cta_note: Violet buttons. CTAs go to the scheduler, the playbook, or a reply to Julia.

mentorship.title: Mentorship Applicants
mentorship.goal: Confirm the application, keep the applicant warm inside the free app until Julia replies, then handle both outcomes (a seat, or not this semester) with the same care. This is the only paid product today, so it gets the most personal treatment.
mentorship.trigger: Voice Application submitted on /mentorship, or started and abandoned.
mentorship.audience: Adults ready to invest a semester in one-on-one work with the founder.
mentorship.cta_note: Gold buttons. Founder voice, first person where possible. Emails 3 and 4 are sent by hand from the CRM.

emails.name: The Mistake Your Ears Miss
emails.timing: Day 2
emails.subject: The mistake your ears miss
emails.preheader: Why sustained notes drift flat, and how to see it.
emails.why: Teaches one concept from the guide in the email itself, so the reader gets value without opening a PDF. The concept chosen (flattening at the end of long notes) is the one Pitch Perfect makes most visible, which makes the CTA feel like the obvious next step.

properties.content:
Mistake #1

Long notes sink. Your ears forgive it.

Most self-taught singers land a note in tune and then let it sag as the breath runs out. By the last beat they are 15 to 30 cents flat, and because it happened slowly, it sounds fine from the inside.

The fix is not more effort. It is seeing the sag, so you can feel the moment support drops.

properties.alt: Pitch Perfect keyboard view: needle, Hz and cents readout on a held C4

properties.content:
Try this

Hold one note for eight slow counts with Pitch Perfect listening. Watch the cents number, not the note name. Where does it start to move?

properties.content:
A thought for your studio

The real problem is between lessons.

A lesson is thirty to sixty minutes. The other six days and twenty-three hours are where a voice actually changes, and most of us teach blind to them.

Students say they practiced. Some did. Some did the wrong thing carefully. Some opened the app once and closed it. Until you can see the difference, every lesson starts with guesswork.

What changes

When practice data arrives before the lesson, the first ten minutes stop being diagnosis and become work.
